newsitem.title: USA: U.S. EPA postpones controversial clean air rules.
newsitem.headline: U.S. EPA postpones controversial clean air rules.

text.p: The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has put off until late summer implementation of controversial tougher clean air standards to allow more time for public comment, the agency said Saturday.

In a letter to the nation's governors at their annual winter meeting in Washington, EPA Administrator Carol Browner said the EPA would extend the public comment period, which was set to expire Feb. 18, for another 60 days. Publication of final rules, which had been set for June, would also be delayed for 60 days, she said.

"I am committed to reviewing these important public health and environmental standards for the American people in a timely manner," Browner wrote. "I also recognise that it is critical for the American people to have a thorough, fair and informed public debate on the EPA proposal."

EPA's proposals to tighten restrictions on allowable levels of smog-producing ozone and airborne particulates have come under fire from businesses and many state officials worried about the cost of the proposed new restrictions. The proposal also for the first time restrict the tiniest particles that can lodge in the lungs.

"We've had a victory that Carol Browner acknowledges that all of us need need to give more time to consideration of these clean air standards," Ohio Gov. George Voinovich, a Republican, said at a news conference Saturday. He has voiced concern that the cost of complying with the stricter clean air rules would outweigh any health benefits.
Administration officials, though, have said the proposed stricter standards would prolong the lives of 20,000 Americans every year and save billions of dollars in health costs.
The EPA proposal would throw dozens of counties that currently meet air quality control standards out of compliance and they would be forced to impose new steps to control pollution.
State and local government worried about the impact of the rules on their budgets asked the EPA last month to give them extra time to comment on the proposed standards.
